title: Undercover Brother
full_review:
An ultra-cool 1970s-style black dude (Eddie Griffin) is enlisted to infiltrate a secret white supremacist organization in the strained Universal comedy "Undercover Brother."

���� The films is based on an animated internet series of the same name and while the colorful costumes and props are a hoot, the threadbare script settles for lowest-common-denominator humor that lacks wit but has comic-book violence to spare.

���� Bemoaning the demise of black culture over the last three decades, members of the goofilyacronymed B.R.O.T.H.E.R.H.O.O.D. plot against the dominant white establishment, known as The Man. When the brothers see a bank videotape of Undercover Brother (Griffin) altering mortgage files to help needy black folks, they convince him to join them. He has to trade in his huge Afro, pork chop sideburns, “UB” monogrammed belt and bell bottoms to disguise himself as a conservative African-American executive who can spy on the enemy up close. Providing back-up is tough, tart SistahGirl (Aunjanue Ellis), but assigned by The Man to seduce and neutralize him is a white seductress (Denise Richards).

���� Billy Dee Williams plays a Colin Powell-like presidential hopeful reduced to running a fried chicken franchise after he is drugged by The Man, which plans to drug his chickens as well. More lame comedy is exemplified by Chris Kattan'srole as a white flunky who unconsciously acts like a hip African-American, much to his distress. Even worse in the acting department are Barbarella-like Richards, and Neil Patrick Harris as the token white in the B.R.O.T.H.E.R.H.O.O.D.

���� Dave Chappelle, Chi McBride and Gary Anthony Williams are also along for the ride, but where the film might have been sassy-smart it ended up silly-stupid. It revels in politically incorrect dialogue and characterizations, and director Malcolm D. Lee resorts to furious fisticuffs every few minutes that are supposed to be comical but look and sound nasty. A goofy, sweet tone might have been a better way to make the exaggerated racial stereotypes in "Undercover Brother" seem like innocuous fun.

���� Due to much comically intended violence, implied drug abuse, sexual references and an instance of rough language. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
